title: Voting in favour estops a delegate from later claiming they did not understand the proposal
content:
A.1.6.6.2 establishes a bright-line evidentiary rule: "An Aligned Delegate who votes in favor of a proposal is deemed to have read and understood the key governance implications of that proposal at the time of voting... the act of voting in favor constitutes affirmative acknowledgment of the proposal's contents and consequences."

The consequence is unusually sharp. "Claims of ignorance, misunderstanding, or failure to read proposal text shall not be accepted as defenses in any subsequent governance proceeding," and "an Aligned Delegate who later claims they did not understand what they voted for commits a Tier 2 breach" — the *defence itself* is the terminal offence. A delegate cannot mitigate a bad vote by pleading inattention; attempting to ends the delegateship.

The asymmetry is deliberate and well-reasoned: "This rule applies only to votes cast in favor. Aligned Delegates who vote against or abstain retain the ability to raise concerns about proposal clarity or their understanding of its implications." Approval is an act with consequences that others rely on, so it carries a representation. Opposition and abstention are exactly how a delegate should register incomplete understanding — and A.1.6.2.1.1 confirms abstention is appropriate where a delegate "lacks sufficient expertise on a specialized matter." The rule channels uncertainty into abstention rather than punishing it.

Two exceptions preserve fairness where the delegate could not have known: the estoppel "does not apply where the proposal text was materially misleading at the time of voting, or where critical facts... emerged after the vote concluded." But "the burden of establishing that the proposal text was misleading or that newly discovered facts are material rests with the Aligned Delegate" — consistent with the inverted burden that governs ACs generally (A.1.5.9.0.4.2).

The systemic function is to make delegated voting power meaningful. Delegation only transfers judgment if the delegate is answerable for exercising it; an ignorance defence would let a delegate collect budget and delegation while disclaiming responsibility for outcomes.
description: A.1.6.6.2 deems a yes vote affirmative acknowledgment of contents and consequences; a later claim of ignorance is itself a Tier 2 breach, and the rule applies only to votes in favour.
